questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
questions.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{2}y\,i+5xy\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨y+2{x}^{2}y,\,{x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}⟩$
across the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and  $(0,1)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/98d7da0c7cd1e1f1006c1db74ae1a1e1f198d9066df6585745ee36548f0b8d96.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy+(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2xy.$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨\sqrt[3]{y}+x,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/ea6c25e40b6683d9ff4a4884dbbda708fd79dbd79d0b50730f9ad6e165d2eb58.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{y}+x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-6{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-6{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(1-6{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-2{x}^{3}y)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(2-2(2)^{3}y)-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-16y)\,dy \\  & =[2y-8{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2(1)-8(1)^{2})-0 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡y-3{x}^{3},\,x{e}^{x}-4x{y}^{3}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle $-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/2696cdadd3cb020cfbe343b9c372893ac18b63f3548ff71003b7328b19de39d5.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y-3{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{e}^{x}-4x{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-9{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-12x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-9{x}^{2}-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-9{x}^{2}-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[-3{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(-3(1)^{3}-6(1)^{2}{y}^{2})-(-3(-1)^{3}-6(-1)^{2}{y}^{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-6)\,dy \\  & =-6y\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)-y{x}^{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+2xy⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(0,-1),(1,-1),(1,0),$ and $(0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/3497b3bbc834879026235f97468f5feb26e91a2b73a4de3da87597bf422ecd33.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)-y{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 0}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{2}-{x}^{2}y)\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[(1-y)-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(1-y)\,dy \\  & =[y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-((-1)-\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2x,\,{x}^{5}-3y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 1,-1\le y\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/35e378bca35f4b0822c713556065415d59b5c566ec8fcc8e3124256aac7b7f14.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{5}-3y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-3)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-(-1))\,dy \\  & =-2{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & =-2y\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{y}+2{x}^{2}y,\,{e}^{x}+2x{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and $(-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/f6437eddec7d44a10c7fb2b3461a09844ca06e5131b69503f51432eb87fedd31.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{y}+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x}+2x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy+4xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}8xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{2}y\,{|}_{-1}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4(2)^{2}y-4(-1)^{2}y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12y\,dy \\  & =6{y}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12x-10)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2y}^{2y}(12x-10)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}-10x]_{-2y}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(24{y}^{2}-20y)-(24{y}^{2}+20y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-40y)\,dy \\  & =-40{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-40(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨x-\sqrt{y},\,y-\sqrt{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/c4dd4d03bdfcf6c3d597e2fdef8681e4f3316b3f276cb9967933b61b0dc90976.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x-\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y-\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(0-(-1)) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},\,{x}^{3}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:

$$

$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/006d80a7dbe4d03b78cc5fb1a642405e3fdfdd69ec9d80014ee8e0355ad1ae73.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y/2}^{y/2}(y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[x]_{-y/2}^{y/2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[\frac{y}{2}-(-\frac{y}{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+y)\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y},\,3{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/f6e80e3010ec7c40d3f59dbb1da4e77c985c889a720b6f954177d8ad83a01351.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=12yx,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12yx+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}(12yx+6y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{y}^{2}x+3{y}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{x}^{2}+3x)\,dx \\  & =(2{x}^{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =22-0 \\  & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨30xy,\,15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=y,$ $\,x=-\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/24369439bc62cf06084a43d97dff0cee4e4089fd103511ef73d9dd5af1256ebb.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=30xy$ and $Q(x,y)=15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=30y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =30y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):\sqrt{y}\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(30y+30y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}60y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y[x]_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}\,dy \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y(y+\sqrt{y})\,dy \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+{y}^{3/2})\,dy \\  & =60{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =60(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{5})-0 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0), (-1,-3), (1,-3),$ and $(1,0),$  traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (7x^2y^6 +x^3)\, \mathbf{i} + (- 2xy^7+4x^2y) \, \mathbf{j}$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/02964b07e45daba2d560fa16d34bcc92ddb8d0e0e83f644f8284dbe9d4b4557b.png)

We have that $P(x,y) =  7x^2y^6 +x^3$ and $Q(x,y) =- 2xy^7+4x^2y.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14x{y}^{6}+3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-14x{y}^{6}+4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -1\leq x\leq 1, \, -3\leq y \leq 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14x{y}^{6}+3{x}^{2})+(-14x{y}^{6}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}7{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle \sin(\pi y) - x , \: \cos(\pi x) + 2xy \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(0,-1), (2,-1), (2,1),$ and $(0,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/2f3374de4a29c62587a79f6286dfe788e64c37e09e9d9b83b3a67b4dac10dc21.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = \sin(\pi y) - x$ and $Q(x,y) = \cos(\pi x) + 2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  0 \leq x \leq 2, \, -1 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}-x)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({2}^{2}-2)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2\,dy \\  & =2y\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2(1)-2(-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0), (2,2),$ and $(-2,2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/aa822f0b9259d6d9eb5c6f439588e70d4b9bee16b2b868fae36c7cbac72d3c3f.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = -3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y+\cos x .$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  -y \leq x \leq y, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)[x]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)(y-(-y))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\cdot 2y\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-6{y}^{3}+2y)\,dy \\  & =[-6\cdot \frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+2\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{3{y}^{4}}{2}+{y}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =(-24+4)-0 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
